message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | Key Rights | How to Exercise Them | |------|------------|----------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after the lease ends, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if you receive a partial refund. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, etc.).
• Must comply with all local building and health codes. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• If the landlord fails to fix issues, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on rent increases, but the landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** for a month‑to‑month lease and **90 days’ notice** for a fixed‑term lease. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• If you’re on a month‑to‑month lease, you can negotiate or move out if the increase is unreasonable. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: Landlord may terminate only for cause (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease). | • Keep written notices and receipts of any payments.
• If you’re evicted, you have the right to contest the eviction in court. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **3‑day notice** for non‑payment of rent, a **30‑day notice** for lease violations, or a **60‑day notice** for ending a month‑to‑month lease.
• After the notice period, the landlord can file an eviction lawsuit. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• File a “Notice to Pay or Quit” or “Notice to Cure” if you’re behind on rent.
• Attend the court hearing; you can present evidence of payment or lease compliance. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entry notices.
• Report unauthorized entries to the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes under the Fair Housing Act. | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time to repair, etc.). | • Keep receipts and document the issue.
• Notify the landlord in writing before making repairs. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease; late fees are allowed only if stated in the lease. | • Pay via a method that provides proof (check, bank transfer, etc.). | | **Lease Renewal** | • Landlord must provide notice of renewal terms at least **30 days** before the lease ends. | • Negotiate renewal terms or request a new lease in writing. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas offers free or low‑cost legal aid for tenants through local bar associations and community organizations. | • Contact the Texas Legal Services Center or local tenant advocacy groups. | #### Quick Tips for Protecting Your Rights 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Understand all clauses, especially those about rent, deposits, and maintenance responsibilities. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written correspondence, and receipts help protect you in disputes. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – Texas law requires specific notice periods for rent increases, lease termination, and entry. 4. **Respond Promptly** – Ignoring notices can lead to eviction or loss of deposit. 5. **Seek Mediation** – Many cities offer mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes before going to court. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. For specific legal questions, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant advocacy organization.
